## The accessibility paradox

For ==type 1 diabetes (T1D)== serious games, scientific evaluation and public availability frequently concern different products. [Reinders et al. (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.diabres.2024.111833) reviewed 21 studies, 23 research-origin games and 13 app-store games. Their audit found:

1. **21 of 23 research-origin games were not publicly available.**
2. No identified web or personal-computer research game could be located.
3. Only one of 11 research mobile games was free in Google Play.
4. All 13 app-store games were visible in Apple’s store, five were visible in Google Play and 11 were free.
5. The public products generally lacked peer-reviewed product-level outcome evaluation.

This is not a simple quality ranking. Research prototypes can generate valuable design and feasibility evidence without becoming distributable products. Public products can be maintained and widely used without having undergone independent comparative evaluation. A useful knowledge base must therefore report **evidence** and **availability** as separate dimensions.

## Point-in-time access snapshot

The entries below are the most accessible core or companion products identified in the 24 August 2026 audit, with selected products rechecked on 5 September 2026. Store and browser access can differ by country, device, operating-system version, account, and transport-security compatibility.

| Product | Access point | Observed status | Cost/account caveat | Evidence caveat |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [AvaType1](https://avatype1.com/) | iOS/iPadOS | Public; active 2026 release | Free; United States listing verified | No peer-reviewed product outcome study located |
| FlightGlucose | Browser | No locally functioning access link on 5 September 2026: both an automated request and a Chromium browser failed during the TLS handshake, although indexed content remained retrievable | Five free scenarios claimed; Learner and Educator subscriptions advertised; direct play not verified | No peer-reviewed outcome study located |
| [GlucoZor](https://www.glucozor.fr/) | Official French site | Site active; mobile-store status incomplete | Free claim | No independent controlled product outcome study located |
| [Level One](https://playlevelone.com/) | iOS/Android | Public | Free; account introduced; full regional coverage not verified | No peer-reviewed product outcome study located |
| [MyDiabetic](https://www.my-diabetic.com/) | iOS/Android | Public | Free; English/Czech | Co-design and short feasibility evidence; no controlled long-term outcome |
| [Rufus](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.sproutel.rufus) | Mobile; optional bear | Public app; update observed December 2025 | App free; physical-bear distribution varies | No controlled product trial located |
| [T1D Simulator](https://krauhe.github.io/t1d-simulator/) | Browser | Public | Free; no account identified | No peer-reviewed educational outcome evidence located |
| [Novi-Chek](https://www.accu-chek.fr/produits/application/novi-chek) | Mobile; French | Official product-information page accessible; tested App Store and Google Play acquisition links returned HTTP 404 | Historically free; present acquisition and regional availability remain incompletely verified | No controlled product trial located |
| [Sweet Strategy](https://apps.apple.com/tw/app/%E7%94%9C-%E6%94%BB%E7%95%A5/id1619470848) | Taiwan iOS | Public regional listing | Free; Traditional Chinese | No independent product outcome evaluation located |
| [eddii](https://www.eddiihealth.com/eddii-app) | United States mobile service | Public | Download and care-service terms differ; real health-data integration | Adjacent management service; independent educational efficacy unestablished |

Publicly accessible experiential works include [Hell Hath No Insulin](https://weeabetes.itch.io/hell-hath-no-insulin), [Permanence](https://ivy-leaves.itch.io/permanence) and [Holesome](https://holesome.itch.io/holesome). These are relevant to lived experience, identity and burden, but no peer-reviewed outcome evaluation was located.

## Why a research game often disappears

### Funding ends before maintenance begins

Research grants commonly fund requirements work, a prototype, recruitment, analysis and publication. Long-term hosting, operating-system updates, app signing, accessibility repair, translation, user support and security response are different recurring activities. They may have no funded owner after the study closes.

### The build is not a citable research object

Articles often describe a game without providing a versioned executable, source repository, installation instructions, licence, archival identifier or maintenance contact. The paper survives; the product does not. This was a recurrent finding in the accessibility audit ([Reinders et al., 2024](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.diabres.2024.111833)).

### Multidisciplinary knowledge is concentrated in people

A credible T1D game can require software engineering, clinical diabetes knowledge, physiology, learning design, game design, accessibility, localisation, privacy governance and lived-experience input. If design rationale and content provenance remain tacit, departure of one researcher or developer can make safe maintenance impractical.

### Proprietary dependencies age quickly

GlucoBoy/DIDGET depended on specialised meters and game hardware. PAL depended on a robot, tablet and dashboard ecosystem. Mobile products depend on developer accounts, store policies, software-development kits and operating-system compatibility. Each dependency creates another termination point.

### Health-data integration raises the operating burden

Products linked to glucose monitoring, insulin data or clinical services require privacy, security, data-retention and therapeutic-boundary decisions. These obligations differ materially from a fictional simulation that does not process personal health data. The distinction should be visible to users and maintainers.

### Localisation is not a one-time translation

Language, food culture, insulin terminology, glucose units, school roles and clinical pathways change the meaning of content. Sustainable localisation requires version control, domain review and a process for propagating scientific corrections across languages.

## Why games are rarely offered during diagnosis education

The literature and product audit support system-level explanations, not an account of any individual clinical encounter:

1. **No stable procurement object:** staff cannot recommend an obsolete build, study login or unsupported device.
2. **Weak product-level evidence:** pooled reviews rarely identify which current product works for which learner.
3. **Paediatric concentration:** many designs may appear irrelevant or patronising to newly diagnosed adults.
4. **Guideline mismatch:** care pathways define educational content but rarely evaluate named games and current versions.
5. **Workflow constraints:** diagnosis education requires short, reliable and explainable resources that fit clinical teaching.
6. **Professional trust:** punitive framing, inaccurate physiology or unclear provenance can make a game difficult to endorse.
7. **Discovery failure:** biomedical databases omit independent games; app stores omit evidence; papers omit surviving access links.
8. **Equity:** hardware, language, region, reading level, disability access and connectivity determine who can participate.

A brochure is easier to print, revise, approve and hand to every patient. That operational advantage does not mean a brochure teaches dynamic causal relationships better; it means the maintenance and governance burden is lower.

## Availability states used in this knowledge base

| State | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Publicly available** | A working official or distribution access point was located at the verification date |
| **Region/device limited** | Access was verified only for a specified store, country, language or hardware environment |
| **Study-only/trial-only** | Access required participation or researcher provision |
| **Research prototype** | A prototype was documented but no public build was located |
| **Archived/historical** | Documentation or lawful historical access information survives, but routine contemporary access does not |
| **Discontinued** | Credible sources indicate that ordinary distribution ended |
| **Uncertain** | Available evidence was insufficient to determine current access |

Price is recorded separately as free, paid, subscription/service-based, historically paid, not applicable or unknown. “Free” never implies absence of data collection, an account, hardware costs or regional restrictions.

## Minimum survival package for future projects

1. **Versioned release:** archive the exact evaluated build and identify its platform requirements.
2. **Open metadata:** publish title history, audience, learning objectives, mechanisms, evidence, access and owner contact in a machine-readable record.
3. **Scientific provenance:** link every clinical or physiological claim to a maintained source register.
4. **Design rationale:** document what each mechanic is intended to teach and how that claim should be evaluated.
5. **Separation of content and code:** make text, translations, scenarios and citations reviewable without specialist code changes.
6. **Sustainable licensing:** use an explicit software and content licence where rights permit; document third-party exclusions.
7. **Low-dependency distribution:** prefer browser or widely supported platforms when the learning objective does not require specialist hardware.
8. **Named stewardship:** define who reviews content, handles security, renews infrastructure and decides when a version should be withdrawn.
9. **Reproducible evaluation:** retain protocols, outcome definitions, analysis code and de-identified aggregate results where lawful.
10. **Succession process:** make contributor onboarding and project transfer possible before the original investigator leaves.

Open source and artificial intelligence may reduce some programming, documentation and localisation costs, but neither substitutes for clinical accountability, user testing, evidence appraisal, privacy governance or a funded maintenance owner.

## Re-verification schedule

1. Check active core products every six months.
2. Check store- and region-limited records from at least two regions where practical.
3. Preserve the previous observation; do not silently overwrite access history.
4. Record the checked URL, date, device/store context and confidence.
5. Change “unavailable” only when a public build is found; change “public” when the access point is actually tested or a credible discontinuation notice is located.
6. Re-run literature searches annually and after a major review publication.

## Image access and republication

The catalogue retains an image source URL, copyright holder and reuse status where these were identifiable. A private scholarly build may display lawfully acquired review copies. A public build should embed only images with adequate permission or licence; otherwise it should provide a labelled link to the official screenshot or source page. Public visibility of an image is not, by itself, republication permission.
